This paper asks whether galaxies at redshift 9 to 10 fall below that local relation. Two problems can blur the test. Lensing may magnify compact glowing gas differently from broader starlight used to estimate mass. The common local comparison is also extrapolated below the stellar mass range where it was calibrated. The core evidence is five strictly un-lensed polyk galaxies from redshift 9.3 to 9.9. Their oxygen abundances use direct electron temperature measurements, which infer gas temperature from an oral line. A DEX is a logarithmic unit. Against the CURDI comparison, the five galaxies average 0.69 plus or minus 0.03 DEX lower in oxygen abundance, leaving about one-fifth the nearby level. Leave one-out tests show a 0.04 DEX spread. Replacing the extrapolated CURDI comparison with the Andrews and Martini relation, measured at these masses, moves the deficit from 0.69 to about 0.65 DEX. The 0.04 DEX shift is roughly 10%. GNZ11 is not among the five core polyk galaxies. It is a separate extension at redshift 10.6 with greater oxygen abundance uncertainty. It confirms the deficit's direction, while the population result remains 0.64 to 0.68 DEX lower. A separate cross check stacks roughly 1,500 un-lensed jades galaxies across redshift 4 to 10. It finds a 0.5 to 0.6 DEX deficit, only one quarter to one-third the nearby abundance. The redshift 9 to 10 value still rests on individual polyk detections. The electron temperature scale remains uncertain by 0.1 to 0.2 DEX. The deficit's direction survives checks, but its size is systematics limited. The star-forming main sequence links stellar mass to how quickly stars form. The mass-metallicity relation links stellar mass to oxygen abundance. This study asks how both change toward the early universe. About 490,000 Sloan Digital Sky Survey Galaxies set the nearby baseline. 180 James Webb Spectroscopic Galaxies provide early star formation. 145 also provide metallicity. Another 3,743 infrared catalog sources add only star formation statistics because they lack metallicity. A calibration turns spectral lines into oxygen abundance. The authors rebuild the nearby benchmark with 200,000 SDSS galaxies on an electron-temperature anchored scale, matching the early sample. Then every early galaxy is compared at the same stellar mass. A DEX is logarithmic. At fixed mass, star formation is 0.77 DEX above nearby galaxies at Redshift 3.5, about 6 times faster. At Redshift 6.7, 1.94 DEX means nearly 90 times faster. The last bin has 46 galaxies above Redshift 6. This James Webb sample favors strong emission lines and unusually intense star formation for each mass. So the reported elevation may be inflated and should be read cautiously. Oxygen deficits are 0.43, 0.37, and 0.40 DEX at Redshift's 4.6, 5.3, and 7.2. Each corresponds to about 40% of nearby oxygen abundance at fixed mass. From Redshift 4 to 7, the median metallicity deficit stays nearly flat. Yet the middle 68% spans 0.5 DEX, about a factor of 3, and some galaxies lie within 0.15 DEX of the nearby relation. The sample is diverse. Roughly 0.1 DEX of calibration uncertainty remains, and the low mass nearby relation is extrapolated. Emission line selection matters. This machine-generated manuscript uses public queries. A galaxy's mass modellicity relation links its stellar mass to the abundance of elements in its gas. This review asks why surveys can disagree before the galaxies differ, then separates three observational effects that are often mixed together. Calibration scale means the conversion from emission line measurements to an abundance. Aperture means how much of a galaxy the instrument samples. Diffuse ionized gas is thinly spread, electrically charged gas. The framework treats these as separate sources of bias. One family of diagnostics uses models of gas ionized by light. Another is anchored to electron temperature. Their absolute oxygen-abundant scales can differ by about 0.7 decks, mathematically a factor of 5. Without conversion, that offset can mimic or hide evolution. Individual line ratio tools also have limits. The R23 indicator can map one reading to two possible abundances. Nitrogen-based indicators assume a local nitrogen-to-oxygen pattern that may fail at high redshift, so mixing diagnostics can create a false trend. A fixed fiber covers different physical areas at different distances. When its samples below roughly 20% of the galaxy, central to global metallicity errors can exceed 0.15 decks. Small central samples can therefore contribute to an apparent high-mass turnover. Diffuse ionized gas supplies 30 to 60% of H alpha, a hydrogen emission line, in the reviewed literature. It's harder ionizing field strengthens low ionization lines. When spectra blend this gas with other emission, inferred changes in metallicity across a galaxy can flatten or even reverse. The recommended workflow has three steps. Put every abundance on one declared scale using published conversions. Require enough galaxy coverage or apply corrections calibrated with spatial maps. Finally, use integral field spectroscopy, which resolves positions across a galaxy as an independent check. This literature-based practitioner framework is not a new metallicity measurement.
